Global well-posedness for a Boussinesq- Navier-Stokes System with critical dissipation

Taoufik Hmidi Address: IRMAR, Université de Rennes 1

Abstract.

In this paper we study a fractional diffusion Boussinesq model which couples a Navier-Stokes type equation with fractional diffusion for the velocity and a transport equation for the temperature. We establish global well-posedness results with rough initial data.

Key words and phrases: 
Boussinesq system, transport equations, paradifferential calculus

1. Introduction

The aim of this paper is to study the global well-posedness for the Boussinesq system with partial fractional dissipation

(1.1) {∂tv+v⋅∇v+|D|​v+∇p=θ​e2∂tθ+v⋅∇θ=0div​v=0v|t=0=v0,θ|t=0=θ0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\partial_{t}v+v\cdot\nabla v+|\textnormal{D}|v+\nabla p=\theta e_{2}\\ \partial_{t}\theta+v\cdot\nabla\theta=0\\ \textnormal{div}\,v=0\\ v_{|t=0}=v^{0},\quad\theta_{|t=0}=\theta^{0}.\end{array}\right.

Here, we focus on the two-dimensional case, the space variable x=(x1,x2)x=(x_{1},x_{2}) is in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, the velocity field vv is given by v=(v1,v2)v=(v^{1},v^{2}) and the pressure pp and the temperature θ\theta are scalar functions. The factor θ​e2\theta e_{2} in the velocity equation, the vector e2e_{2} being given by (0,1)(0,1), models for example the effect of gravity on the fluid motion. The operator |D||\textnormal{D}| stands for the multiplication by |ξ|:=ξ12+ξ22|\xi|:=\sqrt{\xi_{1}^{2}+\xi_{2}^{2}} in the Fourier space.

If we take θ0=0\theta^{0}=0 then the system (1.1) is reduced to the generalized Navier-Stokes system which was studied in a series of papers [24, 25, 26] for all space dimension d≥2.d\geq 2. In particular, for the generalized Navier-Stokes system in dimension two, from the Beale-Kato-Majda criterion [3] and the maximum principle for the vorticity [10], smooth solutions are global in time.

The system (1.1) can be seen as part of the class of generalized Boussinesq systems. These systems under the form

(1.2) {∂tv+v⋅∇v+∇p=θ​e2+𝒟v​v∂tθ+v⋅∇θ=𝒟θ​θdiv​v=0v|t=0=v0,θ|t=0=θ0\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\partial_{t}v+v\cdot\nabla v+\nabla p=\theta e_{2}+\mathcal{D}_{v}v\\ \partial_{t}\theta+v\cdot\nabla\theta=\mathcal{D}_{\theta}\theta\\ \textnormal{div}\,v=0\\ v_{|t=0}=v^{0},\quad\theta_{|t=0}=\theta^{0}\end{array}\right.

are simple models widely used in the modelling of oceanic and atmospheric motions. They also appear in many physical problems, we refer for example to [6] for more details about the modelling issues.

The operators 𝒟v\mathcal{D}_{v} and 𝒟θ\mathcal{D}_{\theta} whose form may vary are used to take into account the possible effects of diffusion and dissipation in the fluid motion.

Mathematically, the simplest model to study is the fully viscous model when 𝒟v=Δ\mathcal{D}_{v}=\Delta, 𝒟θ=Δ.\mathcal{D}_{\theta}=\Delta. The properties of the system are very similar to the one of the two-dimensional Navier-Stokes equation and similar global well-posedness results can be obtained.

The most difficult model for the mathematical study is the inviscid one, i.e. when 𝒟v=𝒟θ=0\mathcal{D}_{v}=\mathcal{D}_{\theta}=0. A local existence result of smooth solution can be proven as for symmetric hyperbolic quasilinear systems, nevertheless, it is not known if smooth solutions can develop singularities in finite time. Indeed, the temperature θ\theta is the solution of a transport equation and the vorticity ω=curl ​v=∂1v2−∂2v1\omega=\mbox{curl }v=\partial_{1}v^{2}-\partial_{2}v^{1} solves the equation

(1.3) ∂tω+v⋅∇ω=∂1θ.\partial_{t}\omega+v\cdot\nabla\omega=\partial_{1}\theta.

The main difficulty is that to get an L∞L^{\infty} estimate on ω\omega which is crucial to prove global existence of smooth solutions for Euler type equation, one needs to estimate ∫0T‖∂1θ‖L∞\int_{0}^{T}||\partial_{1}\theta||_{L^{\infty}} and, unfortunately, no a priori estimate on ∂1θ\partial_{1}\theta is known.

In order to understand the coupling between the two equations in Boussinesq type systems, there have been many recent works studying Boussinesq systems with partial viscosity i.e. with a viscous term acting only in one equation. We refer for example to [2, 7, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16].

In this paper, we shall focus on system (1.1) which corresponds to the case where the heat conductivity is neglected and 𝒟v=−|D|\mathcal{D}_{v}=-|\textnormal{D}|.

When considering the usual Navier-Stokes equation for the velocity, i.e. for 𝒟v=Δ\mathcal{D}_{v}=\Delta, global well-posedness results were recently established in various functional spaces. In [7], Chae proved the global well-posedness for large initial data v0,θ0∈Hsv^{0},\theta^{0}\in H^{s} with s>2.s>2. This result was improved by the first two authors [15] for less regular initial data, that is, v0,θ0∈Hs,v^{0},\theta^{0}\in H^{s}, with s>0.s>0. The uniqueness in the energy space L2L^{2} was recently proved in [13]. According to a recent work of Danchin and Paicu [14] one can construct global unique solution when the dissipation acts only in the horizontal direction: 𝒟v=∂11.\mathcal{D}_{v}=\partial_{11}.

To explain the new difficulties that appear when a weaker diffusion 𝒟v=−|D|α,\mathcal{D}_{v}=-|D|^{\alpha}, α<2\alpha<2 is considered, let us write the system under the vorticity formulation. By using the vorticity defined as the scalar ω=∂1v2−∂2v1,\omega=\partial_{1}v^{2}-\partial_{2}v^{1}, we have to study the system

{∂tω+v⋅∇ω+|D|α​ω=∂1θ,∂tθ+v⋅∇θ=0,ω|t=0=curl v0,θ|t=0=θ0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\partial_{t}\omega+v\cdot\nabla\omega+|\textnormal{D}|^{\alpha}\omega=\partial_{1}\theta,\\ \partial_{t}\theta+v\cdot\nabla\theta=0,\\ \omega_{|t=0}=\textnormal{curl }v^{0},\quad\theta_{|t=0}=\theta^{0}.\end{array}\right.

The standard L2L^{2} energy estimate for this system gives

dd​t​‖ω⁡(t)‖L22+‖ω⁡(t)‖H˙α22≤‖θ⁡(t)‖H˙1−α22,‖θ⁡(t)‖L2=‖θ0‖L2.{d\over dt}\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|\omega(t)\|_{\dot{H}^{\alpha\over 2}}^{2}\leq\|\theta(t)\|_{\dot{H}^{1-{\alpha\over 2}}}^{2},\quad\|\theta(t)\|_{L^{2}}=\|\theta_{0}\|_{L^{2}}.

When α=2\alpha=2, the combination of these two estimates provides the useful information that ω∈Ll​o​c∞​L2∩Ll​o​c2​H˙1.\omega\in L^{\infty}_{loc}L^{2}\cap L^{2}_{loc}\dot{H}^{1}. When α<2\alpha<2 since no a priori estimate on ‖θ‖H˙1−α2\|\theta\|_{\dot{H}^{1-{\alpha\over 2}}} is known some additional work is needed in order to estimate ω\omega. As in [15], the idea would be to use maximal regularity estimates for the semi-group e−t​|D|αe^{-t|\textnormal{D}|^{\alpha}} in order to compensate the loss of one derivative for θ\theta. Nevertheless, some restriction will appear in order to control the nonlinear term. For the sake of clarity, we shall focus on the most difficult case α=1\alpha=1 where this approach would fail: we consider (1.1) for which the vorticity form of the system is

{∂tω+v⋅∇ω+|D|​ω=∂1θ,∂tθ+v⋅∇θ=0,ω|t=0=curl v0,θ|t=0=θ0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\partial_{t}\omega+v\cdot\nabla\omega+|\textnormal{D}|\omega=\partial_{1}\theta,\\ \partial_{t}\theta+v\cdot\nabla\theta=0,\\ \omega_{|t=0}=\textnormal{curl }v^{0},\quad\theta_{|t=0}=\theta^{0}.\end{array}\right.

This is the critical case in the sense that the gain of one derivative by the diffusion term roughly compensates exactly the loss of one derivative in θ\theta in the vorticity equation and has the same order as the convection term.

The main result of this paper is a global well-posedness result for the system (1.1) (see section 2 for the definitions and the basic properties of Besov spaces).

Theorem 1.1.

Let θ0∈L2∩B∞,10\theta^{0}\in L^{2}\cap B_{\infty,1}^{0} and v0v^{0} be a divergence-free vector field belonging to H1∩W˙1,pH^{1}\cap\dot{W}^{1,p} with p∈]2,+∞[.p\in]2,+\infty[. Then the system (1.1) has a unique global solution (v,θ)(v,\theta) such that

v∈Lloc∞​(ℝ+,H1∩W˙1,p)∩Lloc1​(ℝ+,B∞,11)a​n​dθ∈Lloc∞​(ℝ+,L2∩B∞,10).v\in L^{\infty}_{\textnormal{loc}}(\mathbb{R}_{+};H^{1}\cap\dot{W}^{1,p})\cap L^{1}_{\textnormal{loc}}(\mathbb{R}_{+};B_{\infty,1}^{1})\quad and\quad\theta\in L^{\infty}_{\textnormal{loc}}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{2}\cap B_{\infty,1}^{0}).

A few remarks are in order.

Remark 1.2.

From the a priori estimates that we shall get in the proof of Theorem 1.1, it is possible to obtain the existence of various types of global weak solutions, this is discussed in section 5.

At first, it is possible to get the existence without uniqueness of Leray type weak solutions of (1.1) in the energy espace

(v,θ)∈Ll​o​c∞​(ℝ+,L2)∩Ll​o​c2​(ℝ+​H˙12)×Ll​o​c∞​(ℝ+,L2)(v,\theta)\in L^{\infty}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+},L^{2})\cap L^{2}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+}\dot{H}^{1\over 2})\times L^{\infty}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+},L^{2})

by using the energy estimate for the system (1.1). We refer to Proposition 5.1.

We also point out that this system has the following scaling: if (v,θ)(v,\theta) is a solution of (1.1) and λ>0\lambda>0 then (vλ,θλ)(v_{\lambda},\theta_{\lambda}) is also a solution, where vλ​(t,x):=v⁡(λ​t,λ​x)v_{\lambda}(t,x):=v(\lambda t,\lambda x) and θλ​(t,x):=λ​θ​(λ​t,λ​x).\theta_{\lambda}(t,x):=\lambda\theta(\lambda t,\lambda x). As a consequence, the space of initial data H˙1×L2\dot{H}^{1}\times L^{2} which is invariant under this transformation is critical.

From the a priori estimates that we shall establish (see Proposition 5.3), we can also get the existence of global weak solutions (but stronger than the previous ones) by assuming only that v0∈H1v^{0}\in H^{1} and θ0∈L2∩Lr\theta^{0}\in L^{2}\cap L^{r} with r>4r>4 for example i.e. we can get global weak solutions which almost have a critical regularity. Nevertheless the uniqueness for such solutions which do not satisfy the additional regularity assumptions stated in Theorem 1.1 remains unsolved.

Remark 1.3.

Our proof gives more time integrability on the velocity vv. More precisely , we have v∈L~locρ​(ℝ+,B∞,11)v\in\widetilde{L}^{\rho}_{\textnormal{loc}}(\mathbb{R}_{+};B_{\infty,1}^{1}) for all ρ∈[1,p2[.\rho\in[1,\frac{p}{2}[.

Let us say a few words about the main difficulties encountered in the proof of Theorem 1.1. Even if we neglect the nonlinear terms in the Boussinesq system, which reduces the system to the following one

∂tω+|D|​ω=∂1θ,∂tθ=0,\partial_{t}\omega+|\textnormal{D}|\omega=\partial_{1}\theta,\quad\partial_{t}\theta=0,

it is not clear how to perform the standard energy estimate on ω\omega without using neither the control of higher order derivatives of θ\theta nor the maximal regularities of the heat kernel e−t​|D|e^{-t|\textnormal{D}|} which would not be compatible with the nonlinear problem. For example for the L2L^{2} energy estimate, one gets

12​dd​t​‖ω‖L22+‖ω‖H˙122=∫ℝ2∂1θ​ω​𝑑x,‖θ⁡(t)‖L2=‖θ0‖L2,{1\over 2}{d\over dt}\|\omega\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|\omega\|_{\dot{H}^{1\over 2}}^{2}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\partial_{1}\theta\,\omega\,dx,\quad\|\theta(t)\|_{L^{2}}=\|\theta_{0}\|_{L^{2}},

from which no conclusion can be made.

The main idea in the proof of Theorem 1.1, that was also successfully used in the study of the Euler-Boussinesq system [19] is to really use the structural properties of the system solved by (ω,θ)(\omega,\theta). We note that the symbol of the system which is given by

𝒜⁡(ξ)=(−|ξ|−i​ξ100)\mathcal{A}(\xi)=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}-|\xi|&-i\xi_{1}\\ 0&0\end{array}\right)

is diagonalizable for ξ≠0\xi\neq 0 with eigenvalues 00 and −|ξ|-|\xi| which are real and simple. By using the Riesz transform ℛ=∂1|D|\mathcal{R}={\partial_{1}\over|\textnormal{D}|}, one gets that the diagonal form of the system is given by

∂t(ω−ℛ​θ)+|D|​(ω−ℛ​θ)=0,∂tθ=0.\partial_{t}\big(\omega-\mathcal{R}\theta\big)+|\textnormal{D}|\big(\omega-\mathcal{R}\theta\big)=0,\quad\partial_{t}\theta=0.

This last form of the system is much more convenient in order to perform a priori estimates. For example one gets immediately from the continuity on L2L^{2} of ℛ\mathcal{R} that

‖ω⁡(t)‖L2+‖θ⁡(t)‖L2≤C⁡(‖ω0‖L2+‖θ0‖L2).\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{2}}+\|\theta(t)\|_{L^{2}}\leq C\big(\|\omega_{0}\|_{L^{2}}+\|\theta_{0}\|_{L^{2}}\big).

To prove Theorem 1.1, we shall use the same idea, we shall diagonalize the linear part of the system and then get a priori estimates from the study of the new system. The main technical difficulty in this program when one takes the nonlinear terms into account is to evaluate in a sufficiently sharp way the commutator [ℛ,v⋅∇][\mathcal{R},v\cdot\nabla] between the Riesz transform and the convection operator. Such commutator estimates are stated and proven in section 3 of the paper.

The remaining of the paper is organized as follows.

Section 2 is devoted to the definition of the needed functional spaces and the statement of some of their useful properties. Some technical lemmas are also given. Section 3 is devoted to the study of some commutator estimates involving the Riesz transform. Section 4 is dedicated to the study of linear transport-(fractional) diffusion equation. Basically two kind of estimates are given: smoothing effects and logrithmic estimate. In section 5 we discuss a first set of a priori estimates and the issue of weak solutions. Section 6 is dedicated to the proof of Theorem 1.1. The last section is devoted to the proof of some technical lemmas.

3. Riesz transform and commutators

A crucial step in the implementation of the strategy exposed in the introduction for the proof of Theorem 1.1, is the study of commutators between the Riesz transform ℛ=∂1/|D|\mathcal{R}={\partial_{1}}/{|D|} and the convection operator v⋅∇v\cdot\nabla. The results of this section hold for all space dimension d≥2d\geq 2.

Let us first recall some well-known properties of the Riez operator.

Proposition 3.1.

Let ℛ\mathcal{R} be the Riez operator ℛ=∂1/|D|.\mathcal{R}={\partial_{1}}/{|D|}. Then the following hold true.

(1) For every p∈]1,+∞[,p\in]1,+\infty[,

‖ℛ‖ℒ⁡(Lp)≲1.\|\mathcal{R}\|_{\mathcal{L}(L^{p})}\lesssim 1.

(2) Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a fixed ring. Then, there exists ψ∈𝒮\psi\in\mathcal{S} whose spectum does not meet the origin such that

ℛf=2d​qψ(2q⋅)⋆f\mathcal{R}f=2^{dq}\psi(2^{q}\cdot)\star f

for every ff with Fourier transform supported in 2q​𝒞2^{q}\mathcal{C}. In particular, ℛ​Δq\mathcal{R}\Delta_{q} is uniformly bounded (with respct to q∈ℕq\in\mathbb{N}) in LpL^{p} for every p∈[1,+∞].p\in[1,+\infty].

The property (1) is a classical Calderón-Zygmund theorem (see [21] for instance) and (2) is obvious.

The proof of the next lemma is easy and can be found in [19].

Lemma 3.2.

Let p∈[1,∞]p\in[1,\infty], f,gf,g and hh be three functions such that ∇f∈Lp,g∈L∞\nabla f\in L^{p},g\in L^{\infty} and x​h∈L1xh\in L^{1}. Then,

‖h⋆(f​g)−f⁡(h⋆g)‖Lp≤‖x​h‖L1​‖∇f‖Lp​‖g‖L∞.\|h\star(fg)-f(h\star g)\|_{L^{p}}\leq\|xh\|_{L^{1}}\|\nabla f\|_{L^{p}}\|g\|_{L^{\infty}}.

Here is the main result of this section.

Theorem 3.3.

Let vv be is a smooth divergence-free vector field. Then the following hold true.

(1) For every s∈]0,1[s\in]0,1[

∥[ℛ,v]θ∥Hs≲s∥∇v∥L2∥θ∥B∞,2s−1+∥v∥L2∥θ∥L2,\displaystyle\|[\mathcal{R},v]\theta\|_{H^{s}}\lesssim_{s}\|\nabla v\|_{L^{2}}\|\theta\|_{B_{\infty,2}^{s-1}}+\|v\|_{L^{2}}\|\theta\|_{L^{2}},

for every smooth scalar function θ\theta.

(2) For every p∈[2,∞]p\in[2,\infty]

∥[ℛ,v⋅∇]θ∥Bp,∞0≲p∥∇v∥Lp∥θ∥B∞,∞0+∥v∥L2∥θ∥L2,\|[\mathcal{R},v\cdot\nabla]\theta\|_{B_{p,\infty}^{0}}\lesssim_{p}\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\|\theta\|_{B_{\infty,\infty}^{0}}+\|v\|_{L^{2}}\|\theta\|_{L^{2}},

for every smooth scalar function θ\theta.

Proof of Theorem 3.3.

(1) We split the commutator into three parts, according to Bony’s decomposition

[ℛ,v]​θ\displaystyle[\mathcal{R},v]\theta =\displaystyle= ∑q∈ℕ[ℛ,Sq−1​v]​Δq​θ+∑q∈ℕ[ℛ,Δq​v]​Sq−1​θ\displaystyle\sum_{q\in\mathbb{N}}[\mathcal{R},S_{q-1}v]\Delta_{q}\theta+\sum_{q\in\mathbb{N}}[\mathcal{R},\Delta_{q}v]S_{q-1}\theta
+\displaystyle+ ∑q≥−1[ℛ,Δq​v]​Δ~q​θ\displaystyle\sum_{q\geq-1}[\mathcal{R},\Delta_{q}v]\widetilde{\Delta}_{q}\theta
=\displaystyle= ∑q∈ℕIq+∑q∈ℕIIq+∑q≥−1IIIq\displaystyle\sum_{q\in\mathbb{N}}\mbox{I}_{q}+\sum_{q\in\mathbb{N}}\mbox{II}_{q}+\sum_{q\geq-1}\mbox{III}_{q}
=\displaystyle= I+II+III.\displaystyle\mbox{I}+\mbox{II}+\mbox{III}.

∙\bullet Estimation of I. According to the point (2) of Proposition 3.1 there exists h∈𝒮h\in\mathcal{S} whose Fourier transform does not contain the origin such that

Iq​(x)=hq⋆(Sq−1​v​Δq​θ)−Sq−1​v​(hq⋆Δq​θ),\mbox{I}_{q}(x)=h_{q}\star(S_{q-1}v\Delta_{q}\theta)-S_{q-1}v(h_{q}\star\Delta_{q}\theta),

where hq​(x)=2d​q​h​(2q​x)h_{q}(x)=2^{dq}h(2^{q}x). Applying Lemma 3.2 with p=2p=2 we infer

(3.1) ‖Iq‖L2\displaystyle\|\mbox{I}_{q}\|_{L^{2}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∥xhq∥L1∥∇Sq−1v∥L2∥Δqθ∥L∞\displaystyle\|xh_{q}\|_{L^{1}}\|\nabla S_{q-1}v\|_{L^{2}}\|\Delta_{q}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim 2−q​‖∇v‖L2​‖Δq​θ‖L∞.\displaystyle 2^{-q}\|\nabla v\|_{L^{2}}\|\Delta_{q}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}.

In the last line we have used the fact that ‖x​hq‖L1=2−q​‖x​h‖L1\|xh_{q}\|_{L^{1}}=2^{-q}\|xh\|_{L^{1}}. Since for every q∈ℕq\in\mathbb{N} the Fourier transform of Iq\hbox{I}_{q} is supported in a ring of size 2q2^{q} then

‖I‖Hs2≃∑q22​q​s​‖Iq‖L22.\|\hbox{I}\|_{H^{s}}^{2}\simeq\sum_{q}2^{2qs}\|\hbox{I}_{q}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}.

Combined with (3.1) this yields

‖I‖Hs2≲‖∇v‖L22​‖θ‖B∞,2s−12.\displaystyle\|\hbox{I}\|_{H^{s}}^{2}\lesssim\|\nabla v\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\|\theta\|_{B_{\infty,2}^{s-1}}^{2}.

∙\bullet Estimation of II. As before we can write

IIq​(x)=hq⋆(Sq−1​θ​Δq​v)−Sq−1​θ​(hq⋆Δq​v),\mbox{II}_{q}(x)=h_{q}\star(S_{q-1}\theta\Delta_{q}v)-S_{q-1}\theta(h_{q}\star\Delta_{q}v),

and again by Lemma 3.2 with p=2p=2 we obtain

‖IIq‖L2\displaystyle\|\hbox{II}_{q}\|_{L^{2}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖∇v‖L2​2−q​‖Sq−1​θ‖L∞\displaystyle\|\nabla v\|_{L^{2}}2^{-q}\|S_{q-1}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖∇v‖L2​2−q​∑j≤q−2‖Δj​θ‖L∞.\displaystyle\|\nabla v\|_{L^{2}}2^{-q}\sum_{j\leq q-2}\|\Delta_{j}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}.

Thus,

2q​s∥IIq∥L2≲∥∇v∥L2(2(1−s)⋅⋆2(1−s)⋅∥Δ⋅θ∥L∞)(q).\displaystyle 2^{qs}\|\hbox{II}_{q}\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim\|\nabla v\|_{L^{2}}\big(2^{(1-s)\cdot}\star 2^{(1-s)\cdot}\|\Delta_{\cdot}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}\big)(q).

where ⋆\star is the discrete convolution in ℕ∪{−1}\mathbb{N}\cup\{-1\}.

Here again the Fourier transform of IIq\mbox{II}_{q} is supported in a ring of size 2q2^{q} and by consequences ∥II∥Hs≃∥2s⋅∥I⋅∥L2∥ℓ2\|\mbox{II}\|_{H^{s}}\simeq\big\|2^{s\cdot}\|\hbox{I}_{\cdot}\|_{L^{2}}\big\|_{\ell^{2}}. Combined with () and discrete Young inequalities (remember s<1s<1) this yields

‖II‖Hs\displaystyle\|\mbox{II}\|_{H^{s}} ≲s\displaystyle\lesssim_{s} ∥∇v∥L22∥2(s−1)⋅∥Δ⋅θ∥L∞∥ℓ2\displaystyle\|\nabla v\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\big\|2^{(s-1)\cdot}\|\Delta_{\cdot}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}\big\|_{\ell^{2}}
≃\displaystyle\simeq ‖∇v‖L2​‖θ‖B∞,2s−1.\displaystyle\|\nabla v\|_{L^{2}}\|\theta\|_{B_{\infty,2}^{s-1}}.

III=∑q≥1[ℛ,Δq​v]​Δ~q​θ+∑q≤0[ℛ,Δq​v]​Δ~q​θ:=J1+J2.{\rm III}=\sum_{q\geq 1}[\mathcal{R},\Delta_{q}v]\widetilde{\Delta}_{q}\theta+\sum_{q\leq 0}[\mathcal{R},\Delta_{q}v]\widetilde{\Delta}_{q}\theta:=J_{1}+J_{2}.

‖[ℛ,Δq​v]​Δ~q​θ‖L2≲2−q​‖∇v‖L2​‖Δ~q​θ‖L∞.\displaystyle\|[\mathcal{R},\Delta_{q}v]\widetilde{\Delta}_{q}\theta\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim 2^{-q}\|\nabla v\|_{L^{2}}\|\widetilde{\Delta}_{q}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}.

2j​s​‖Δj​J1‖L2≲‖∇v‖L2​∑q≥j−42(j−q)​s​2q⁡(s−1)​‖Δ~q​θ‖L∞2^{js}\|\Delta_{j}J_{1}\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim\|\nabla v\|_{L^{2}}\sum_{q\geq j-4}2^{(j-q)s}2^{q(s-1)}\|\widetilde{\Delta}_{q}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}

Since s>0s>0 then the convolution inequality leads to

‖J1‖Hs\displaystyle\|J_{1}\|_{H^{s}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖∇v‖L2​‖θ‖B∞,2s−1.\displaystyle\|\nabla v\|_{L^{2}}\|\theta\|_{B_{\infty,2}^{s-1}}.

J2J_{2} contains a finite number of terms with low frequencies and it can be handled without using the commutator structure. Indeed, from Bernstein inequalities and the L2L^{2}-continuity of the Riesz transform we obtain for q≤0q\leq 0

‖[ℛ,Δq​v]​Δq​θ‖L2\displaystyle\|[\mathcal{R},\Delta_{q}v]\Delta_{q}\theta\|_{L^{2}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖Δq​v‖L2​(‖Δq​θ‖L∞+‖ℛ​Δq​θ‖L∞)\displaystyle\|\Delta_{q}v\|_{L^{2}}\big(\|\Delta_{q}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|\mathcal{R}\Delta_{q}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}\big)
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖v‖L2​(‖θ‖L2+‖ℛ​θ‖L2)\displaystyle\|v\|_{L^{2}}\big(\|\theta\|_{L^{2}}+\|\mathcal{R}\theta\|_{L^{2}}\big)
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖v‖L2​‖θ‖L2.\displaystyle\|v\|_{L^{2}}\|\theta\|_{L^{2}}.

‖J2‖Hs≲‖v‖L2​‖θ‖L2.\|J_{2}\|_{H^{s}}\lesssim\|v\|_{L^{2}}\|\theta\|_{L^{2}}.

This ends the proof of (1).

(2) We use again Bony’s decomposition to write

[ℛ,v⋅∇]θ\displaystyle[\mathcal{R},v\cdot\nabla]\theta =\displaystyle= ∑q∈ℕ[ℛ,Sq−1v⋅∇]Δqθ+∑q∈ℕ[ℛ,Δqv⋅∇]Sq−1θ\displaystyle\sum_{q\in\mathbb{N}}[\mathcal{R},S_{q-1}v\cdot\nabla]\Delta_{q}\theta+\sum_{q\in\mathbb{N}}[\mathcal{R},\Delta_{q}v\cdot\nabla]S_{q-1}\theta
+\displaystyle+ ∑q≥−1[ℛ,Δqv⋅∇]Δ~qθ\displaystyle\sum_{q\geq-1}[\mathcal{R},\Delta_{q}v\cdot\nabla]\widetilde{\Delta}_{q}\theta
=\displaystyle= I+II+III.\displaystyle\mbox{I}+\mbox{II}+\mbox{III}.

Similarly to (3.1) we have

∥[ℛ,Sq−1v⋅∇]Δqθ∥Lp\displaystyle\big\|[\mathcal{R},S_{q-1}v\cdot\nabla]\Delta_{q}\theta\big\|_{L^{p}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim 2−q∥∇v∥Lp∥Δq∇θ∥L∞\displaystyle 2^{-q}\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\|\Delta_{q}\nabla\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖∇v‖Lp​‖Δq​θ‖L∞.\displaystyle\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\|\Delta_{q}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}.

Thus we get

‖I‖Bp,∞0≲‖∇v‖Lp​‖θ‖B∞,∞0.\|{\rm I}\|_{B_{p,\infty}^{0}}\lesssim\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\|\theta\|_{B_{\infty,\infty}^{0}}.

For the second term we have

∥[ℛ,Δqv⋅∇]Sq−1θ∥Lp\displaystyle\big\|[\mathcal{R},\Delta_{q}v\cdot\nabla]S_{q-1}\theta\big\|_{L^{p}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim 2−q∥∇Δqv∥Lp∥Sq−1∇θ∥L∞\displaystyle 2^{-q}\|\nabla\Delta_{q}v\|_{L^{p}}\|S_{q-1}\nabla\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}

∥III∥Bp,∞0≲∑q≤1∥[ℛ,Δqv⋅∇]Δ~qθ∥Lp+∥∑q≥2div[ℛ,Δqv]Δ~qθ∥Bp,∞0.\displaystyle\|{\rm III}\|_{B_{p,\infty}^{0}}\lesssim\sum_{q\leq 1}\|[\mathcal{R},\Delta_{q}v\cdot\nabla]\widetilde{\Delta}_{q}\theta\|_{L^{p}}+\big\|\sum_{q\geq 2}{\rm div}[\mathcal{R},\Delta_{q}v]\widetilde{\Delta}_{q}\theta\big\|_{B_{p,\infty}^{0}}.

4. Transport-Diffusion models

This section contains some estimates needed in the proof of Theorem 1.1. We start with the following Besov space estimate for the transport equation, for the proof see for example [2].

Proposition 4.1.

Let vv be a smooth divergence-free vector field. Then, every scalar solution ψ\psi of the equation

∂tψ+v⋅∇ψ=f,ψ∣t=0=ψ0,\partial_{t}\psi+v\cdot\nabla\psi=f,\quad\psi_{\mid t=0}=\psi^{0},

satifies, for every p∈[1,+∞]p\in[1,+\infty],

‖ψ⁡(t)‖Bp,∞−1≤C​exp⁡(C​∫0t‖v⁡(τ)‖B∞,11​𝑑τ)​(‖ψ0‖Bp,∞−1+∫0t‖f⁡(τ)‖Bp,∞−1​𝑑τ).\|\psi(t)\|_{B_{p,\infty}^{-1}}\leq C\exp\big(C\int^{t}_{0}\|v(\tau)\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{1}}d\tau\big)\Big(\|\psi^{0}\|_{B_{p,\infty}^{-1}}+\int_{0}^{t}\|f(\tau)\|_{B_{p,\infty}^{-1}}d\tau\Big).

The second proposition is dedicated to some logarithmic and LpL^{p} estimates.

Proposition 4.2.

Let vv be a smooth divergence-free vector field, κ∈ℝ+\kappa\in\mathbb{R}_{+} and (p,r)∈[1,∞]2(p,r)\in[1,\infty]^{2}. Then there exists C>0C>0, such that every scalar solution of

(4.1) ∂tψ+v⋅∇ψ+κ|D|ψ=f,ψ∣t=0=ψ0,\partial_{t}\psi+v\cdot\nabla\psi+\kappa|\textnormal{D}|\psi=f,\quad\psi_{\mid t=0}=\psi^{0},

satisfies

‖ψ‖L~t∞​Bp,r0≤C⁡(‖ψ0‖Bp,r0+‖f‖L~t1​Bp,r0)​(1+∫0t‖∇v​(τ)‖L∞​𝑑τ),\|\psi\|_{\widetilde{L}^{\infty}_{t}B_{p,r}^{0}}\leq C\Big(\|\psi^{0}\|_{B_{p,r}^{0}}+\|f\|_{\widetilde{L}^{1}_{t}B_{p,r}^{0}}\Big)\Big(1+\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla v(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}d\tau\Big),

and

‖ψ⁡(t)‖Lp≤‖ψ0‖Lp+∫0t‖f⁡(τ)‖Lp​𝑑τ.\|\psi(t)\|_{L^{p}}\leq\|\psi^{0}\|_{L^{p}}+\int_{0}^{t}\|f(\tau)\|_{L^{p}}d\tau.

The first result was first proved by Vishik in [23] for the case κ=0\kappa=0 by using the special structure of the transport equation. In [17] the first two authors have generalized Vishik result for a transport-diffusion equation where the dissipation term takes the form −κ​Δ​ψ-\kappa\Delta\psi. The method described in [17] can be easily adapted to the model (4.1), for more details the complete proof can be found in [19]. The LpL^{p} estimates are proved in [10].

In the proof of the uniqueness part of the main theorem we shall also need some estimates for the linearized velocity equation.

Proposition 4.3.

Let vv a smooth divergence free vector field, s∈]−1,1[s\in]-1,1[ and ρ∈[1,∞].\rho\in[1,\infty]. Let uu be a smooth solution of the system

(LB)∂tu+v⋅∇u+|D|​u+∇p=f,div​u=0.{\rm(LB)}\qquad\qquad\partial_{t}u+v\cdot\nabla u+|\textnormal{D}|u+\nabla p=f,\qquad{\rm div}u=0.

Then, we have for every t∈ℝ+t\in\mathbb{R}_{+}

‖u‖Lt∞​B2,∞s≤C​eC​V​(t)​(‖u0‖B2,∞s+‖f‖L~tρ​B2,∞s−1+1ρ​(1+t1−1ρ)),\|u\|_{L^{\infty}_{t}{B}_{2,\infty}^{s}}\leq Ce^{CV(t)}\Big(\|u^{0}\|_{{B}_{2,\infty}^{s}}+\|f\|_{\widetilde{L}^{\rho}_{t}B_{2,\infty}^{s-1+\frac{1}{\rho}}}(1+t^{1-\frac{1}{\rho}}\big)\Big),

where V⁡(t):=∫0t‖∇v​(τ)‖L∞​𝑑τ.V(t):=\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla v(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}d\tau.

dd​t∥uq(t)∥L2+c2q∥uq(t)∥L2≤∥[Δq,v⋅∇]u(t)∥L2+∥fq(t)∥L2.\frac{d}{dt}\|u_{q}(t)\|_{L^{2}}+c2^{q}\|u_{q}(t)\|_{L^{2}}\leq\|[\Delta_{q},v\cdot\nabla]u(t)\|_{L^{2}}+\|f_{q}(t)\|_{L^{2}}.

∥uq(t)∥L2≲e−c​t​2q∥uq0∥L2+∫0te−c​2q​(t−τ)(∥[Δq,v⋅∇]u(τ)∥L2+∥fq(τ)∥L2)dτ\|u_{q}(t)\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim e^{-ct2^{q}}\|u_{q}^{0}\|_{L^{2}}+\int_{0}^{t}e^{-c2^{q}(t-\tau)}\Big(\|[\Delta_{q},v\cdot\nabla]u(\tau)\|_{L^{2}}+\|f_{q}(\tau)\|_{L^{2}}\Big)d\tau

(4.2) supq∈ℕ2q​s∥uq∥Lt∞​L2≲∥u0∥B2,∞s+∫0tsupq∈ℕ2q​s∥[Δq,v⋅∇]u(τ)∥L2dτ+∥f∥L~tρ​B2,∞s−1+1ρ.\sup_{q\in\mathbb{N}}2^{qs}\|u_{q}\|_{L^{\infty}_{t}L^{2}}\lesssim\|u^{0}\|_{B_{2,\infty}^{s}}+\int_{0}^{t}\sup_{q\in\mathbb{N}}2^{qs}\|[\Delta_{q},v\cdot\nabla]u(\tau)\|_{L^{2}}d\tau+\|f\|_{\widetilde{L}^{\rho}_{t}B_{2,\infty}^{s-1+\frac{1}{\rho}}}.

≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖∇v​(t)‖L∞​‖u⁡(t)‖B2,∞s+‖Δ−1​f​(t)‖L2\displaystyle\|\nabla v(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\|u(t)\|_{B_{2,\infty}^{s}}+\|\Delta_{-1}f(t)\|_{L^{2}}

It follows

‖Δ−1​u​(t)‖L2\displaystyle\|\Delta_{-1}u(t)\|_{L^{2}} ≤\displaystyle\leq ‖Δ−1​u0‖L2+∫0t‖∇v​(τ)‖L∞​‖u⁡(τ)‖B2,∞s​𝑑τ+‖Δ−1​f‖Lt1​L2\displaystyle\|\Delta_{-1}u^{0}\|_{L^{2}}+\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla v(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}\|u(\tau)\|_{B_{2,\infty}^{s}}d\tau+\|\Delta_{-1}f\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{2}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖u0‖B2,∞s+∫0t‖∇v​(t)‖L∞​‖u⁡(τ)‖B2,∞s​𝑑τ+t1−1ρ​‖f‖L~tρ​B2,∞s−1+1ρ.\displaystyle\|u^{0}\|_{B_{2,\infty}^{s}}+\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla v(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\|u(\tau)\|_{B_{2,\infty}^{s}}d\tau+t^{1-\frac{1}{\rho}}\|f\|_{\widetilde{L}^{\rho}_{t}B_{2,\infty}^{s-1+\frac{1}{\rho}}}.

The outcome is

‖u⁡(t)‖B2,∞s≲‖u0‖B2,∞s+∫0t‖∇v​(t)‖L∞​‖u⁡(τ)‖B2,∞s​𝑑τ+(1+t1−1ρ)​‖f‖L~tρ​B2,∞s−1+1ρ.\|u(t)\|_{B_{2,\infty}^{s}}\lesssim\|u^{0}\|_{B_{2,\infty}^{s}}+\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla v(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\|u(\tau)\|_{B_{2,\infty}^{s}}d\tau+(1+t^{1-\frac{1}{\rho}})\|f\|_{\widetilde{L}^{\rho}_{t}B_{2,\infty}^{s-1+\frac{1}{\rho}}}.

The proof of the next proposition can be done in a similar way as Theorem 1.2 in [1].

where V⁡(t)=‖∇v‖Lt1​L∞.V(t)=\|\nabla v\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{\infty}}.

5. Weak solutions

Throughout the coming sections we use the notation Φk\Phi_{k} to denote any function of the form

OPENΦk​(t)=C0​exp⁡(…​expCLOSE⏟k​t​i​m​e​s​(C0​t)​…),\Phi_{k}(t)=C_{0}\underbrace{\exp(...\exp}_{k\,times}(C_{0}t)...),

where C0C_{0} depends on the involved norms of the initial data and its value may vary from line to line up to some absolute constants. We will make an intensive use (without mentionning it) of the following trivial facts

∫0tΦk​(τ)​𝑑τ≤Φk​(t)andexp⁡(∫0tΦk​(τ)​𝑑τ)≤Φk+1​(t).\int_{0}^{t}\Phi_{k}(\tau)d\tau\leq\Phi_{k}(t)\qquad{\rm and}\qquad\exp({\int_{0}^{t}\Phi_{k}(\tau)d\tau})\leq\Phi_{k+1}(t).

In this section we shall establish a first set of a priori estimates and discuss some results about weak solutions which are easy consequences. These a priori estimates are also needed in order to construct the global strong solutions as stated in Theorem 1.1.

The first result is concerned with weak solutions in the energy space.

Proposition 5.1.

Let (v0,θ0)∈L2×L2,(v^{0},\theta^{0})\in L^{2}\times L^{2}, then there exists a global weak solution of (1.1) in the space Lloc∞​(ℝ+,L2)∩Lloc2​(ℝ+,H˙12)×L∞​(ℝ+,L2)L^{\infty}_{\textnormal{loc}}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{2})\cap L^{2}_{\textnormal{loc}}(\mathbb{R}_{+};\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}})\times L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{2}) such that

‖v⁡(t)‖L22+∫0t‖v⁡(τ)‖H˙122​𝑑τ\displaystyle\|v(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\int_{0}^{t}\|v(\tau)\|_{\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}}^{2}d\tau ≤\displaystyle\leq C0​(1+t2)\displaystyle C_{0}(1+t^{2})
‖θ⁡(t)‖L2\displaystyle\|\theta(t)\|_{L^{2}} ≤\displaystyle\leq ‖θ0‖L2.\displaystyle\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{2}}.

If in addition, θ0∈Lp\theta^{0}\in L^{p} for some p∈[1,∞]p\in[1,\infty], then there is a weak solution which satisfies also

‖θ⁡(t)‖Lp≤‖θ0‖Lp.\|\theta(t)\|_{L^{p}}\leq\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{p}}.
Proof of Proposition 5.1.

The estimate of θ\theta in LpL^{p} is a consequence of the incompressibility of the flow. The L2L^{2} energy estimate for the velocity can be obtained by taking the L2L^{2}-inner product of the velocity equation in the Boussinesq system with vv,

12​dd​t​‖v⁡(t)‖L22+∫0t‖v⁡(τ)‖H˙122​𝑑τ\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\|v(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\int_{0}^{t}\|v(\tau)\|_{\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}}^{2}d\tau ≤\displaystyle\leq ‖v⁡(t)‖L2​‖θ⁡(t)‖L2\displaystyle\|v(t)\|_{L^{2}}\|\theta(t)\|_{L^{2}}
≤\displaystyle\leq ‖v⁡(t)‖L2​‖θ0‖L2.\displaystyle\|v(t)\|_{L^{2}}\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{2}}.

Thus we obtain

‖v⁡(t)‖L2\displaystyle\|v(t)\|_{L^{2}} ≤\displaystyle\leq ‖v0‖L2+∫0t‖θ⁡(τ)‖L2​𝑑τ\displaystyle\|v^{0}\|_{L^{2}}+\int_{0}^{t}\|\theta(\tau)\|_{L^{2}}d\tau
≤\displaystyle\leq ‖v0‖L2+‖θ0‖L2​t.\displaystyle\|v^{0}\|_{L^{2}}+\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{2}}t.

Inserting this inequality into the previous one leads to the desired estimate. Now to construct global solution we can proceed in a classical way using the Friedrichs method. We omit here the details and for complete description of this method we refer for example to [12]. ∎

Remark 5.2.

Due to the weak regularity of the velocity, the uniqueness problem for these weak solutions seems an interesting widely open problem.

Now we aim at constructing global weak solutions for more regular initial data near the scaling space H˙1×L2\dot{H}^{1}\times L^{2} described in the introduction of this paper.

Proposition 5.3.

Let (v0,θ0)∈H1×L2∩Lr,(v^{0},\theta^{0})\in H^{1}\times L^{2}\cap L^{r}, with r∈]4,∞].r\in]4,\infty]. Then, there exists a global weak solution (v,θ)(v,\theta) for the system (1.1) such that

‖ω⁡(t)‖L22+∫0t‖(ω−ℛ​θ)​(τ)‖H˙122​𝑑τ≤Φ1​(t),\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\int_{0}^{t}\|(\omega-\mathcal{R}\theta)(\tau)\|_{\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}}^{2}d\tau\leq\Phi_{1}(t),

where ω=curl ​v\omega=\mbox{curl }v.

Remark 5.4.

From the estimate of Proposition 5.3 we see that we have an additional smoothing effect for the quantity ω−ℛ​θ\omega-\mathcal{R}\theta since θ\theta belongs only to the space Lt∞​(L2∩Lr)L^{\infty}_{t}(L^{2}\cap L^{r}). This phenomenon illustrates the strong coupling between the velocity and the temperature.

Proof of Proposition 5.3.

We shall, here again, restrict ourselves to the proof of the a priori estimates. The construction of global solutions can be done by following [12]. As explained in the introduction we do not have any available obvious LpL^{p} estimate for the vorticity. Thus in order to get some LpL^{p} estimates we write the Boussinesq system under its diagonal form. For this purpose we set Γ=ω−ℛ​θ.\Gamma=\omega-\mathcal{R}\theta. Then we get from (1.1)

(5.1) (∂t+v⋅∇+|D|)Γ=[ℛ,v⋅∇]θ.(\partial_{t}+v\cdot\nabla+|\textnormal{D}|)\Gamma=[\mathcal{R},v\cdot\nabla]\theta.

By using the identity [ℛ,v⋅∇]θ=div([ℛ,v]θ)[\mathcal{R},v\cdot\nabla]\theta=\textnormal{div}\big([\mathcal{R},v]\theta\big) and a standard L2L^{2} energy estimate, we find

12​dd​t​‖Γ⁡(t)‖L22+‖Γ⁡(t)‖H˙122\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\|\Gamma(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|\Gamma(t)\|_{\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}}^{2} =\displaystyle= ∫ℝ2div​([ℛ,v]​θ)​(t,x)​Γ​(t,x)​𝑑x\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\textnormal{div}\big([\mathcal{R},v]\theta\big)(t,x)\Gamma(t,x)dx
≤\displaystyle\leq ‖[ℛ,v]​θ​(t)‖H˙12​‖Γ⁡(t)‖H˙12.\displaystyle\big\|[\mathcal{R},v]\theta(t)\big\|_{\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}}\|\Gamma(t)\|_{\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}}.

From Theorem 3.3 and Proposition 5.1 we have

‖[ℛ,v]​θ​(t)‖H˙12\displaystyle\big\|[\mathcal{R},v]\theta(t)\big\|_{\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖∇v​(t)‖L2​‖θ⁡(t)‖B∞,2−12+‖v⁡(t)‖L2​‖θ⁡(t)‖L2\displaystyle\|\nabla v(t)\|_{L^{2}}\|\theta(t)\|_{B_{\infty,2}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}+\|v(t)\|_{L^{2}}\|\theta(t)\|_{L^{2}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖ω⁡(t)‖L2​‖θ⁡(t)‖Lr+(1+t).\displaystyle\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{2}}\|\theta(t)\|_{L^{r}}+(1+t).
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖ω⁡(t)‖L2​‖θ0‖Lr+(1+t).\displaystyle\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{2}}\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{r}}+(1+t).

Here, we have used that ‖∇v‖L2≈‖ω‖L2\|\nabla v\|_{L^{2}}\approx\|\omega\|_{L^{2}} and the continuous embedding Lr↪B∞,2−12,L^{r}\hookrightarrow B_{\infty,2}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, for every r>4r>4. Thus we get

‖[ℛ,v]​θ​(t)‖H˙12≲‖ω⁡(t)‖L2+(1+t).\displaystyle\big\|[\mathcal{R},v]\theta(t)\big\|_{\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}}\lesssim\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{2}}+(1+t).

However, the L2L^{2}-continuity of ℛ\mathcal{R} and the conservation of the L2L^{2} norm of θ\theta yield together

‖ω⁡(t)‖L2\displaystyle\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{2}} ≤\displaystyle\leq ‖Γ⁡(t)‖L2+‖ℛ​θ​(t)‖L2\displaystyle\|\Gamma(t)\|_{L^{2}}+\|\mathcal{R}\theta(t)\|_{L^{2}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖Γ⁡(t)‖L2+‖θ0‖L2.\displaystyle\|\Gamma(t)\|_{L^{2}}+\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{2}}.

Collecting the previous estimates, we find

12​dd​t​‖Γ⁡(t)‖L22+‖Γ⁡(t)‖H˙122≲(‖Γ⁡(t)‖L2+1+t)​‖Γ⁡(t)‖H˙12.\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\|\Gamma(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|\Gamma(t)\|_{\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}}^{2}\lesssim\big(\|\Gamma(t)\|_{L^{2}}+1+t\big)\|\Gamma(t)\|_{\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}}.

It follows from the Young inequality that

dd​t​‖Γ⁡(t)‖L22+‖Γ⁡(t)‖H˙122≤C0​‖Γ⁡(t)‖L22+C0​(1+t2).\frac{d}{dt}\|\Gamma(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|\Gamma(t)\|_{\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}}^{2}\leq C_{0}\|\Gamma(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+C_{0}(1+t^{2}).

After an Integration in time and the use of the Gronwall inequality we obtain

‖Γ⁡(t)‖L22+∫0t‖Γ⁡(τ)‖H˙122​𝑑τ\displaystyle\|\Gamma(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\int_{0}^{t}\|\Gamma(\tau)\|_{\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}}^{2}d\tau ≤\displaystyle\leq C0​(1+t2)​eC0​t\displaystyle C_{0}\big(1+t^{2}\big)e^{C_{0}t}
≤\displaystyle\leq Φ1​(t).\displaystyle\Phi_{1}(t).

This ends the proof of the claimes a priori estimate in Proposition 5.3.

6. Proof of Theorem 1.1

The proof of Theorem 1.1 will be done in three steps. First we prove other a priori estimates for the equations (1.1). Second, we prove the uniqueness part. Finally, we discuss the construction of the solutions.

6.1. A priori estimates

We have already proven some a priori estimates in Proposition 5.1 and Proposition 5.3. In the sequel we shall prove some other estimates. To estimate the LpL^{p} norm of ω\omega we have to distinguish two cases. If p∈]2,4[p\in]2,4[ then we can prove this estimate in one step. If not, we establish first an estimate of the LrL^{r} norms of ω\omega for all r∈]2,4[r\in]2,4[ and then11 1 Notice that, concerning the velocity, the assumptions of Theorem 1.1 are equivalent to v0∈L2v^{0}\in L^{2} and ω0∈Lr\omega^{0}\in L^{r} for all r∈[2,p],r\in[2,p], for some p∈]2,+∞[p\in]2,+\infty[. use it to get a smoothing effect on the quantity (ω−ℛ​θ)(\omega-\mathcal{R}\theta). This will in turn yield the crucial estimate on the Lipschitz norm of the velocity. Finally, by using the estimate on the lipschitz norm of the velocity, one can easily propagate the LpL^{p} norm of the vorticity and conclude the subsection about the a priori estimates.

Proposition 6.1.

Let (v,θ)(v,\theta) be a solution of the Boussinesq system (1.1) such that v0∈H1∩W˙1,pv^{0}\in H^{1}\cap\dot{W}^{1,p} and θ0∈L2∩L∞\theta^{0}\in L^{2}\cap L^{\infty} with p∈]2,+∞[.p\in]2,+\infty[. Then,

‖ω⁡(t)‖Lrr+∫0t‖(ω−ℛ​θ)​(τ)‖L2​rr​𝑑τ≤Φ1​(t),\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{r}}^{r}+\int_{0}^{t}\|(\omega-\mathcal{R}\theta)(\tau)\|_{L^{2r}}^{r}d\tau\leq\Phi_{1}(t),

for every r∈[2,4[∩[2,p].r\in[2,4[\cap[2,p].

Proof of Proposition 6.1.

Multiplying (5.1) by |Γ|r−2​Γ|\Gamma|^{r-2}\Gamma and integrating in space variable we get for every s∈]0,1[s\in]0,1[ (ss will be carefully chosen later)

(6.1) 1r​dd​t​‖Γ⁡(t)‖Lrr+∫ℝ2(|D|​Γ)​|Γ|r−2​Γ​𝑑x\displaystyle\frac{1}{r}\frac{d}{dt}\|\Gamma(t)\|_{L^{r}}^{r}+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(|\textnormal{D}|\Gamma)\,|\Gamma|^{r-2}\Gamma dx =\displaystyle= ∫ℝ2div​([ℛ,v]​θ)​|Γ|r−2​Γ​𝑑x\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\textnormal{div}\big([\mathcal{R},v]\theta\big)|\Gamma|^{r-2}\Gamma dx
≤\displaystyle\leq ‖[ℛ,v]​θ​(t)‖H˙1−s​‖|Γ|r−2​Γ​(t)‖H˙s.\displaystyle\big\|[\mathcal{R},v]\theta(t)\big\|_{\dot{H}^{1-s}}\||\Gamma|^{r-2}\Gamma(t)\|_{\dot{H}^{s}}.

According to Lemma 3.3 in [18] one has

2r​‖|Γ|r2‖H˙122≤∫ℝ2(|D|​Γ)​|Γ|r−2​Γ​𝑑x.\frac{2}{r}\||\Gamma|^{\frac{r}{2}}\|_{\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}}^{2}\leq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(|\textnormal{D}|\Gamma)\,|\Gamma|^{r-2}\Gamma dx.

Combining this estimate with the Sobolev embedding H˙12↪L4,\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}\hookrightarrow L^{4}, we find

(6.2) ‖Γ‖L2​rr≲∫ℝ2(|D|​Γ)​|Γ|r−2​Γ​𝑑x.\|\Gamma\|_{L^{2r}}^{r}\lesssim\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(|\textnormal{D}|\Gamma)\,|\Gamma|^{r-2}\Gamma dx.

To estimate the RHS of (6.1), we use the following lemma (see the appendix for the proof).

Lemma 6.2.

Let β∈[2,+∞[\beta\in[2,+\infty[ and s∈]0,1[s\in]0,1[.Then, we have

‖|u|β−2​u‖H˙s≲‖u‖L2​ββ−2​‖u‖H˙s+1−2β,\||u|^{\beta-2}u\|_{\dot{H}^{s}}\lesssim\|u\|_{L^{2\beta}}^{\beta-2}\|u\|_{\dot{H}^{s+1-\frac{2}{\beta}}},

for every smooth function u.u.

Combined with (6.1) and (6.2) this lemma yields

≤\displaystyle\leq Φ1​(t)​‖θ⁡(t)‖B∞,2−s+C0​(1+t2).\displaystyle\Phi_{1}(t)\|\theta(t)\|_{{B}_{\infty,2}^{-s}}+C_{0}(1+t^{2}).

It suffices now to use the embedding L∞↪B∞,2−sL^{\infty}\hookrightarrow{B}_{\infty,2}^{-s} for s>0.s>0. and Proposition 5.1 to get that

Therefore

dd​t​‖Γ⁡(t)‖Lrr+c​‖Γ⁡(t)‖L2​rr≤Φ1​(t)​‖Γ‖L2​rr−2​‖Γ‖H˙12.\frac{d}{dt}\|\Gamma(t)\|_{L^{r}}^{r}+c\|\Gamma(t)\|_{L^{2r}}^{r}\leq\Phi_{1}(t)\|\Gamma\|_{L^{2r}}^{r-2}\|\Gamma\|_{\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}}.

|a​b|≤C​|a|r2+c2​|b|rr−2|ab|\leq C|a|^{\frac{r}{2}}+\frac{c}{2}|b|^{\frac{r}{r-2}}

we get

After integration in time and the application of the Hölder inequality (remember that r<4r<4), we find

(6.3) ‖Γ⁡(t)‖Lrr+∫0t‖Γ⁡(τ)‖L2​rr​𝑑τ\displaystyle\|\Gamma(t)\|_{L^{r}}^{r}+\int_{0}^{t}\|\Gamma(\tau)\|_{L^{2r}}^{r}d\tau ≤\displaystyle\leq Φ1​(t)​(∫0t‖Γ⁡(τ)‖H˙122​𝑑τ)r/4+‖Γ0‖Lrr\displaystyle\Phi_{1}(t)\big(\int_{0}^{t}\|\Gamma(\tau)\|_{\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}}^{2}d\tau\big)^{r/4}+\|\Gamma^{0}\|_{L^{r}}^{r}
≤\displaystyle\leq Φ1​(t).\displaystyle\Phi_{1}(t).

In the last line we have used Proposition 5.3. ∎

Next we give a smoothing effect for the quantity Γ\Gamma which will be the keystone of a Lipschitz control of the velocity.

Proposition 6.3.

Under the assumptions of Proposition 6.1 we have

‖ω−ℛ​θ‖L~tρ​Br,12r≤Φ1​(t),\|\omega-\mathcal{R}\theta\|_{\widetilde{L}^{\rho}_{t}B_{r,1}^{\frac{2}{r}}}\leq\Phi_{1}(t),

Proof of Proposition 6.3.

For q∈ℕq\in\mathbb{N} we set Γq=Δq​Γ.\Gamma_{q}=\Delta_{q}\Gamma. Then, we localize in frequencies the equation (5.1) for Γ\Gamma to get

6.3. Existence

We consider the following system

(Bn) {∂tvn+vn⋅∇vn+|D|​vn+∇pn=θn​e2∂tθn+vn⋅∇θn=0div​vn=0vn|t=0=Snv0,θn|t=0=Snθ0\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\partial_{t}v_{n}+v_{n}\cdot\nabla v_{n}+|\textnormal{D}|v_{n}+\nabla p_{n}=\theta_{n}e_{2}\\ \partial_{t}\theta_{n}+v_{n}\cdot\nabla\theta_{n}=0\\ \textnormal{div}v_{n}=0\\ {v_{n}}_{|t=0}=S_{n}v^{0},\quad{\theta_{n}}_{|t=0}=S_{n}\theta^{0}\end{array}\right.

First remark that Sn​v0,Sn​θ0∈Hs,∀s∈ℝS_{n}v^{0},S_{n}\theta^{0}\in H^{s},\forall s\in\mathbb{R} since v0,θ0∈L2.v^{0},\theta^{0}\in L^{2}. As in the classical theory of quasi-linear hyperbolic systems, we can prove the local well-posedness of the system (Bn{\rm B}_{n}). The global well-posedness is related to the following criterion: the solution can be continued beyond the time TT if the quantity ‖∇vn‖LT1​L∞\|\nabla v_{n}\|_{L^{1}_{T}L^{\infty}} is finite. Now from the a priori estimates, in particular Proposition 6.6, the Lipschitz norm of the velocity can not blow up in finite time and hence the solution (vn,θn)(v_{n},\theta_{n}) is globally defined. Once again from the a priori estimates we have for 1≤ρ<p/21\leq\rho<{p}/{2}

‖vn‖LT∞​(H1∩W˙1,p)+‖vn‖LTρ​B∞,11≤Φ2​(T),\|v_{n}\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}(H^{1}\cap\dot{W}^{1,p})}+\|v_{n}\|_{L^{\rho}_{T}B_{\infty,1}^{1}}\leq\Phi_{2}(T),

and

‖θn‖LT∞​(L2∩B∞,10)≤Φ2​(T).\|\theta_{n}\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}(L^{2}\cap B_{\infty,1}^{0})}\leq\Phi_{2}(T).

It follows that up to the extraction of a subsequence (vn,θn)(v_{n},\theta_{n}) is weakly convergent to (v,θ)(v,\theta) satisfying the same estimate as above. Now using (6.18) we get the following: if we have

an,m=‖(Sn−Sm)​v0‖B2,∞0+‖(Sn−Sm)​θ0‖B2,∞−1≤α⁡(T)a_{n,m}=\|(S_{n}-S_{m})v^{0}\|_{B_{2,\infty}^{0}}+\|(S_{n}-S_{m})\theta^{0}\|_{B_{2,\infty}^{-1}}\leq\alpha(T)

then

‖vn−vm‖LT∞​B2,∞0+‖θn−θm‖LT∞​B2,∞−1≤β⁡(T)​(an,m)γ⁡(T).\displaystyle\|v_{n}-v_{m}\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}B_{2,\infty}^{0}}+\|\theta_{n}-\theta_{m}\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}B_{2,\infty}^{-1}}\leq\beta(T)\big(a_{n,m}\big)^{\gamma(T)}.

This proves that (vn)(v_{n}) is a Cauchy sequence and hence that it converges strongly to vv in the space LT∞​B2,∞0.L^{\infty}_{T}B_{2,\infty}^{0}. By interpolation we can easily get the strong convergence of vnv_{n} to vv in L2​([0,T]×ℝ2)L^{2}([0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^{2}). This implies that vn⊗vnv_{n}\otimes v_{n} converges in L1​([0,T]×ℝ2)L^{1}([0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^{2}). But since θn\theta_{n} converges to θ\theta weakly in L2​([0,T]×ℝ2)L^{2}([0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^{2}) then, by weak strong convergence, we have also that vn​θnv_{n}\,\theta_{n} converges weakly to v​θv\,\theta.

This allows us to pass to the limit in the system (Bn)({\rm B}_{n}) and to get that (v,θ)(v,\theta) is a solution of our initial problem.

Appendix: some technical lemmas

Here we restate and prove Lemma 6.2.

Lemma 6.9.

Let β∈[2,+∞[\beta\in[2,+\infty[, s∈]0,1[s\in]0,1[ and u∈L2​β∩H˙s+1−2βu\in L^{2\beta}\cap\dot{H}^{s+1-\frac{2}{\beta}}. Then we have

‖|u|β−2​u‖H˙s≲‖u‖L2​ββ−2​‖u‖H˙s+1−2β.\||u|^{\beta-2}u\|_{\dot{H}^{s}}\lesssim\|u\|_{L^{2\beta}}^{\beta-2}\|u\|_{\dot{H}^{s+1-\frac{2}{\beta}}}.
Proof.

We shall actually establish the more accurate estimate:

‖|u|β−2​u‖H˙s≤C​‖u‖L2​ββ−2​‖u‖B˙β,2s.\||u|^{\beta-2}u\|_{\dot{H}^{s}}\leq C\|u\|_{L^{2\beta}}^{\beta-2}\|u\|_{\dot{B}_{\beta,2}^{s}}.

Once this estimate is established, the result follows from the embedding H˙s+1−2β↪B˙β,2s,\dot{H}^{s+1-\frac{2}{\beta}}\hookrightarrow\dot{B}_{\beta,2}^{s}, for β≥2\beta\geq 2 which is an easy consequence of Bernstein inequalities. For 0<s<10<s<1, we can use the characterization of the homogeneous Sobolev space H˙s,\dot{H}^{s},

(6.19) ‖|u|β−2​u‖H˙s2≈∫ℝ2∥|u|β−2u(x−⋅)−|u|β−2u(⋅)∥L22|x|2+2​s​𝑑x.\big\||u|^{\beta-2}u\big\|_{\dot{H}^{s}}^{2}\approx\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\frac{\||u|^{\beta-2}u(x-\cdot)-|u|^{\beta-2}u(\cdot)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{|x|^{2+2s}}dx.

On the other hand there exists CC depending on β\beta such that for every a,b∈ℝa,b\in\mathbb{R}

||a|β−2​a−|b|β−2​b|≤C​|a−b|​(|a|β−2+|b|β−2).\big||a|^{\beta-2}a-|b|^{\beta-2}b\big|\leq C|a-b|\big(|a|^{\beta-2}+|b|^{\beta-2}\big).

Thus using this inequality and integrating in yy we get by Cauchy-Schwarz inequality

∥|u|β−2u(x−⋅)−|u|β−2u(⋅)∥L2≤C∥u(x−⋅)−u(⋅)∥Lβ∥u∥L2​ββ−2.\||u|^{\beta-2}u(x-\cdot)-|u|^{\beta-2}u(\cdot)\|_{L^{2}}\leq C\|u(x-\cdot)-u(\cdot)\|_{L^{\beta}}\|u\|_{L^{2\beta}}^{\beta-2}.

Inserting this estimate into (6.19) and using the characterization of Besov space leads to

‖|u|β−2​u‖H˙s2\displaystyle\||u|^{\beta-2}u\|_{\dot{H}^{s}}^{2} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖u‖L2​β2​β−4​∫ℝ2∥u(x−⋅)−u(⋅)∥Lβ2|x|2+2​s​𝑑x\displaystyle\|u\|_{L^{2\beta}}^{2\beta-4}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\frac{\|u(x-\cdot)-u(\cdot)\|_{L^{\beta}}^{2}}{|x|^{2+2s}}dx
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖u‖L2​β2​β−4​‖u‖B˙β,2s2.\displaystyle\|u\|_{L^{2\beta}}^{2\beta-4}\|u\|_{\dot{B}_{\beta,2}^{s}}^{2}.

This concludes the proof. ∎

Lemma 6.10 (Commutators estimates).

Let vv be a smooth divergence-free vector field and ff be a smooth function then

  1. (1)

    for every q≥−1q\geq-1

    ∥[Δq,v⋅∇]f∥Lp≲∥∇v∥Lp∥f∥B∞,∞0.\|[\Delta_{q},v\cdot\nabla]f\|_{L^{p}}\lesssim\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\|f\|_{B_{\infty,\infty}^{0}}.
  2. (2)

    For every s∈[−1,0]s\in[-1,0]

    ‖v⋅∇f‖B2,∞s≲‖v‖L2​‖f‖B∞,11+s.\|v\cdot\nabla f\|_{B_{2,\infty}^{s}}\lesssim\|v\|_{L^{2}}\|f\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{1+s}}.
Proof.

(1) We shall actually prove the refined estimate

∥[Δq,v⋅∇]θ∥Lp≲∥∇v∥Lp∥θ∥B∞,∞0.\|[\Delta_{q},v\cdot\nabla]\theta\|_{L^{p}}\lesssim\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\|\theta\|_{B_{\infty,\infty}^{0}}.

The desired estimate will follow from the embedding Bp,12p↪B∞,∞0.B_{p,1}^{\frac{2}{p}}\hookrightarrow B_{\infty,\infty}^{0}. We have from Bony’s decomposition

[Δq,v⋅∇]θ\displaystyle[\Delta_{q},v\cdot\nabla]\theta =\displaystyle= ∑|j−q|≤4[Δq,Sj−1v⋅∇]Δjθ+∑|j−q|≤4[Δq,Δjv⋅∇]Sj−1θ\displaystyle\sum_{|j-q|\leq 4}[\Delta_{q},S_{j-1}v\cdot\nabla]\Delta_{j}\theta+\sum_{|j-q|\leq 4}[\Delta_{q},\Delta_{j}v\cdot\nabla]S_{j-1}\theta
+\displaystyle+ ∑j≥q−4[Δq,Δjv⋅∇]Δ~jθ\displaystyle\sum_{j\geq q-4}[\Delta_{q},\Delta_{j}v\cdot\nabla]\widetilde{\Delta}_{j}\theta
:⁣=\displaystyle:= Iq+IIq+IIIq.\displaystyle\mbox{I}_{q}+\mbox{II}_{q}+\mbox{III}_{q}.

Observe first that

Iq=∑|j−q|≤4hq⋆(Sj−1v⋅∇Δjθ)−Sj−1v⋅(hq⋆∇Δjθ)\mbox{I}_{q}=\sum_{|j-q|\leq 4}h_{q}\star(S_{j-1}v\cdot\nabla\Delta_{j}\theta)-S_{j-1}v\cdot(h_{q}\star\nabla\Delta_{j}\theta)

where h^q​(ξ)=φ⁡(2−q​ξ)\hat{h}_{q}(\xi)=\varphi({2^{-q}}\xi). Thus, Lemma 3.2 and Bernstein inequalities yield

‖Iq‖Lp\displaystyle\|\mbox{I}_{q}\|_{L^{p}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∑|j−q|≤4∥xhq∥L1∥∇Sj−1v∥Lp∥∇Δjθ∥L∞\displaystyle\sum_{|j-q|\leq 4}\|xh_{q}\|_{L^{1}}\|\nabla S_{j-1}v\|_{L^{p}}\|\nabla\Delta_{j}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖∇v‖Lp​‖h0‖L1​∑|j−q|≤42j−q​‖Δj​θ‖L∞\displaystyle\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\|h_{0}\|_{L^{1}}\sum_{|j-q|\leq 4}2^{j-q}\|\Delta_{j}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖∇v‖Lp​‖θ‖B∞,∞0.\displaystyle\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\|\theta\|_{B_{\infty,\infty}^{0}}.

To estimate the second term we use once again Lemma 3.2

‖IIq‖Lp\displaystyle\|\hbox{II}_{q}\|_{L^{p}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∑|j−q|≤42−q∥Δj∇v∥Lp∥∇Sj−1θ∥L∞\displaystyle\sum_{|j-q|\leq 4}2^{-q}\|\Delta_{j}\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\|\nabla S_{j-1}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖∇v‖Lp​∑|j−q|≤4k≤j−22k−q​‖Δk​θ‖L∞\displaystyle\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\sum_{|j-q|\leq 4\atop k\leq j-2}2^{k-q}\|\Delta_{k}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖∇v‖Lp​‖θ‖B∞,∞0.\displaystyle\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\|\theta\|_{B_{\infty,\infty}^{0}}.

Let us now move to the remainder term. We separate it into two terms: high frequencies and low frequencies.

IIIq\displaystyle\hbox{III}_{q} =\displaystyle= ∑j≥q−4j∈ℕ[Δq∂i,Δjvi]Δ~jθ+[Δq,Δ−1v⋅∇]Δ~−1θ\displaystyle\sum_{j\geq q-4\atop j\in\mathbb{N}}[\Delta_{q}\partial_{i},\Delta_{j}v^{i}]\widetilde{\Delta}_{j}\theta+[\Delta_{q},\Delta_{-1}v\cdot\nabla]\widetilde{\Delta}_{-1}\theta
:⁣=\displaystyle:= IIIq1+IIIq2.\displaystyle\hbox{III}_{q}^{1}+\hbox{III}_{q}^{2}.

For the first term we don’t need to use the structure of the commutator. We estimate separately each term of the commutator by using Bernstein inequalities.

‖IIIq1‖Lp\displaystyle\|\hbox{III}_{q}^{1}\|_{L^{p}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∑j≥q−4j∈ℕ2q​‖Δj​v‖Lp​‖Δ~j​θ‖L∞\displaystyle\sum_{j\geq q-4\atop j\in\mathbb{N}}2^{q}\|\Delta_{j}v\|_{L^{p}}\|\widetilde{\Delta}_{j}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖∇v‖Lp​∑j≥q−42q−j​‖Δ~j​θ‖L∞\displaystyle\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\sum_{j\geq q-4}2^{q-j}\|\widetilde{\Delta}_{j}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖∇v‖Lp​‖θ‖B∞,∞0.\displaystyle\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\|\theta\|_{B_{\infty,\infty}^{0}}.

For the second term we use Lemma 3.2 combined with Bernstein inequalities.

‖IIIq2‖Lp\displaystyle\|\hbox{III}_{q}^{2}\|_{L^{p}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∥∇Δ−1v∥Lp∥∇Δ~−1θ∥L∞\displaystyle\|\nabla\Delta_{-1}v\|_{L^{p}}\|\nabla\widetilde{\Delta}_{-1}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖∇v‖Lp​‖θ‖B∞,∞0.\displaystyle\|\nabla v\|_{L^{p}}\|\theta\|_{B_{\infty,\infty}^{0}}.

(2) According to by Bony’s decompostion and div​v=0\hbox{div}v=0

v⋅∇u=Tvi​∂iu+T∂iu​vi+∂iℛ⁡(vi,u).v\cdot\nabla u=T_{v^{i}}\partial_{i}u+T_{\partial_{i}u}v^{i}+\partial_{i}\mathcal{R}(v^{i},u).

To estimate the first term we write by definition

2q​s​‖Δq​(Tvi​∂iu)‖L2≲∑|j−q|≤42j+q​s​‖Sj−1​v‖L2​‖Δj​u‖L∞.2^{qs}\|\Delta_{q}(T_{v^{i}}\partial_{i}u)\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim\sum_{|j-q|\leq 4}2^{j+qs}\|S_{j-1}v\|_{L^{2}}\|\Delta_{j}u\|_{L^{\infty}}.

Now we use the inequality

‖Sj−1​v‖L2≤‖v‖L2.\|S_{j-1}v\|_{L^{2}}\leq\|v\|_{L^{2}}.

Thus we get

supq2q​s​‖Δq​(Tvi​∂iu)‖L2≲‖v‖L2​‖u‖B∞,∞1+s.\sup_{q}2^{qs}\|\Delta_{q}(T_{v^{i}}\partial_{i}u)\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim\|v\|_{L^{2}}\|u\|_{B_{\infty,\infty}^{1+s}}.

Straightforward calculus gives since 1+s≤0,1+s\leq 0,

2q​s​‖Δq​(T∂iu​vi)‖L2\displaystyle 2^{qs}\|\Delta_{q}(T_{\partial_{i}u}v^{i})\|_{L^{2}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∑|j−q|≤4k≤j−12j⁡(1+s)​‖Δk​u‖L∞​‖Δj​v‖L2\displaystyle\sum_{|j-q|\leq 4\atop k\leq j-1}2^{j(1+s)}\|\Delta_{k}u\|_{L^{\infty}}\|\Delta_{j}v\|_{L^{2}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖v‖L2​‖u‖B∞,11+s.\displaystyle\|v\|_{L^{2}}\|u\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{1+s}}.

and

‖∂iℛ⁡(vi,u)‖B2,∞s≲‖v‖L2​‖u‖B∞,11+s.\|\partial_{i}\mathcal{R}(v^{i},u)\|_{B_{2,\infty}^{s}}\lesssim\|v\|_{L^{2}}\|u\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{1+s}}.

∎

Lemma 6.11.

Let v∈H1v\in H^{1} then we have

‖v‖L2≲‖v‖B2,∞0​log⁡(e+‖v‖H1‖v‖B2,∞0).\|v\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim\|v\|_{B_{2,\infty}^{0}}\log\Big(e+\frac{\|v\|_{H^{1}}}{\|v\|_{B_{2,\infty}^{0}}}\Big).
Proof.

Let N∈ℕ∗N\in\mathbb{N}^{*} be a fixed number then using the dyadic decomposition we get

‖v‖L2\displaystyle\|v\|_{L^{2}} ≤\displaystyle\leq ∑q≤N−1‖Δq​v‖L2+∑q≥N‖Δq​v‖L2\displaystyle\sum_{q\leq N-1}\|\Delta_{q}v\|_{L^{2}}+\sum_{q\geq N}\|\Delta_{q}v\|_{L^{2}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim N​‖v‖B2,∞0+2−N​‖v‖H1.\displaystyle N\|v\|_{B_{2,\infty}^{0}}+2^{-N}\|v\|_{H^{1}}.

Choosing

N=[log2⁡(e+‖v‖H1/‖v‖B2,∞0)]N=\Big[\log_{2}\Big(e+\|v\|_{H^{1}}/\|v\|_{B_{2,\infty}^{0}}\Big)\Big]

gives the desired result. ∎
